title: World falling short on 22 of 23 nature targets for 2030, says draft UN report - Carbon Brief
gist: A second draft of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity's global progress report finds countries falling short on 22 of 23 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework targets for 2030, with only the climate-biodiversity target scoring 'green'. The biggest gaps are in finance mobilisation ($186.4bn cumulative against a $200bn/year goal) and harmful-subsidy reform, setting up a contentious global review at COP17 in Armenia in October 2026.

themes.theme: GBF scorecard: 22 of 23 targets off track

insights.claim: A draft UN Convention on Biological Diversity global report concludes the 2030 mission to halt and reverse biodiversity loss will not be achieved unless collective implementation accelerates rapidly.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Signals that nature-related regulation will be renegotiated rather than enforced at COP17; expect pressure for new corporate disclosure and finance mandates rather than target rollback.
insights.quote: However, unless collective implementation accelerates rapidly, the 2030 targets and mission will not be achieved.
insights.locator: Overall findings

insights.claim: Countries have taken some action on all 23 Global Biodiversity Framework targets, but the report states that no target presents a fully positive picture, with only one target scoring in the 'green' 0.75-1 band.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A near-universal miss means nature policy is entering an enforcement/accountability phase - watch for mandatory rather than voluntary corporate nature reporting.

insights.claim: The only target awarded a 'green' score is target 8, on minimising the impact of climate change on biodiversity through mitigation, adaptation and nature-based solutions.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Climate-nature convergence is the one area with policy momentum - nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based adaptation providers sit in the least-contested niche of the nature agenda.
insights.locator: Overall findings

insights.claim: The report identifies two distinct gaps: an ambition gap, where national targets do not fully reflect the scope of the global targets, and an implementation gap, where countries are not acting enough to hit even their own weaker targets.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A useful diagnostic for judging any national nature pledge: check both whether the target maps to the global one and whether spending backs it.
insights.locator: Overall findings

insights.claim: Progress is described as particularly lagging on the indirect drivers of biodiversity loss - harmful business practices and the government subsidies that promote them - rather than on direct conservation measures.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The political economy, not the science, is the binding constraint; sectors dependent on nature-harming subsidies face slow, negotiated rather than abrupt reform risk.

insights.claim: Countries show consistent gaps in protecting marine, coastal and inland water ecosystems, making ocean and freshwater the weakest link across the framework.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Marine and freshwater conservation is where the funding gap is widest - relevant for blue-finance instruments and marine protected area programmes.

insights.claim: The evidence base itself is incomplete: only 45% of countries published national biodiversity strategies in time for the report, 83% submitted at least one national target and 66% produced a new national report.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Any headline claim about global nature progress rests on partial reporting - treat aggregate biodiversity statistics as lower bounds with a selection bias toward better performers.

insights.claim: The flagship '30 by 30' target to protect 30% of Earth's land and sea is seeing progress in protected-area expansion, especially marine and coastal, but current ambition and implementation remain insufficient to fully achieve it.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Marine protected area designation is the fastest-moving sub-sector of the nature agenda; land-based 30x30 is where shortfalls concentrate.

insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Paper parks risk: protected-area coverage stats are a weak proxy for conservation outcomes and for social-licence risk in project finance.

insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The flagship target lacks domestic legal anchoring in most countries - do not price in binding national land-use restrictions from 30x30 alone.

insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Restoration is a volume story without a quality standard yet - a gap that carbon and biodiversity credit methodologies could monetise.

themes.theme: Harmful subsidies: the $500bn reform that is not happening

insights.claim: Target 18 requires countries to identify biodiversity-harmful subsidies by 2025 and cut them by at least $500bn per year by 2030, but overall progress is judged insufficient.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The single largest financial lever in the nature framework is stalling - agriculture, fisheries and fossil-linked subsidy recipients face little near-term policy shock.
insights.locator: Subsidies

insights.claim: Only 27% of countries address the $500bn annual subsidy reduction in national targets and just 5% set quantitative national subsidy-reduction targets.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Almost no country has made subsidy reform measurable, so the 2030 $500bn goal is effectively unenforceable - low regulatory risk, high credibility risk for the framework.
insights.locator: Just 27%, however, address the issue

insights.claim: Only one-quarter of national targets highly aligned with the subsidy target are on track, with most showing insufficient progress, and several national reports cite entrenched interests and political barriers to subsidy reform.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Incumbent lobbying is explicitly named as the blocker - subsidy-dependent agricultural and extractive incumbents retain pricing support longer than policy targets imply.
insights.quote: entrenched interests and political barriers to subsidy reform

insights.claim: Just 22 countries reported the value of their biodiversity-harmful subsidies, totalling $268bn over 2022-2025, averaging $67bn a year - orders of magnitude below the trillions estimated to be spent annually.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Reported subsidy figures are severe undercounts; the true stock of nature-harming public support dwarfs any conservation finance being mobilised.

insights.claim: Carbon Brief's own analysis, using a wider set of 32 country submissions, put harmful subsidies at roughly $270bn a year versus the report's $67bn annual average - showing how much the number moves with sample size.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Methodology drives the headline: be sceptical of any single global harmful-subsidy figure quoted without its country sample.

insights.claim: Harmful subsidies may have fallen around 20% in recent years among the minority of countries reporting consistently over 2022-24, yet their total value still exceeds the resources countries reported mobilising for biodiversity.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Nature finance is still net-negative at the public-policy level - conservation inflows are outweighed by harmful outflows, a structural drag on any nature-positive thesis.

insights.claim: Goal D frames a $700bn annual biodiversity finance gap to be closed by 2030 through $500bn of subsidy reform plus $200bn a year mobilised from all sources.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The architecture assumes most of the gap closes via subsidy removal, not new money - so failure on subsidies mechanically blows out the finance gap.

insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Biodiversity finance is running at roughly a quarter of the required annual run-rate - the funding gap is a persistent, not closing, opportunity and risk.

insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: North-to-south nature finance is running roughly four to five times below the pledged level, keeping developing-country conservation dependent on debt and private capital.

insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Diplomatic softening of the draft is a tell that COP17 will avoid formally declaring failure - the political narrative will be more optimistic than the underlying data.

insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Nature funding is overwhelmingly domestic and fiscally squeezed - it is a budget line that tracks sovereign fiscal space, not international pledges.

insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Rearmament and food-security budgets are directly crowding out conservation spending - a concrete channel from geopolitics to nature-sector funding.

insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The private nature-finance market that the EU pushed to include in target 19 has stalled post-2021; biodiversity credit and debt-for-nature markets are pre-scale, not scaling.

themes.theme: Genetic data, the Cali Fund and benefit-sharing

insights.claim: Only $6.9m in cumulative monetary receipts from the use of genetic resources was reported across 2022-2025, with several parties reporting no monetary benefits at all.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Benefit-sharing from genetic data is currently a rounding error - pharma, biotech and agri-genomics face negligible near-term payment obligations but rising legal-framework risk.
insights.locator: For those that have tracked benefits

insights.claim: The Cali Fund agreed at COP16 for companies profiting from digital sequence information is voluntary, and as of December 2025 had received a single $1,000 'icebreaker' contribution with no major companies following.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Voluntary corporate nature funds are not attracting capital; expect pressure to shift toward binding national access-and-benefit-sharing laws instead.
insights.locator: In December 2025, Carbon Brief reported

insights.claim: The most fundamental regulatory barrier cited by countries is the absence of dedicated national frameworks covering access to genetic resources, digital registries, tracking systems and a financial mechanism to pay communities.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Regulatory build-out - registries, traceability and payment rails for genetic data - is an unbuilt infrastructure layer with obvious software and compliance demand.
insights.locator: Genetic resources

insights.claim: Countries reported more than 960 non-monetary benefits from genetic resources, such as technical training and research participation, but these fluctuated over time rather than increasing and are not indicative of global benefit-sharing.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Non-monetary benefit counts are being used to pad a benefit-sharing record with almost no cash flowing - discount them in assessing compliance progress.

themes.theme: Pollution and invasive species: measurement failure as the binding constraint

insights.claim: On target 7, 60% of highly aligned national pollution targets show no significant change or insufficient progress and only 35% are on track for 2030.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Pesticide and nutrient regulation is progressing far slower than the halving pledge implies - limited near-term demand shock for agrochemical inputs.
insights.locator: The draft report finds that there is no significant change

insights.claim: Just five countries out of 125 submitted estimates on pesticide concentrations in the environment, and only one country has met the aim of halving overall pesticide risk nationally.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Enforcement of the pesticide-halving goal is effectively non-existent for lack of data; agrochemical regulatory risk stays low into 2030 absent an EU-style national push.
insights.locator: Just five countries out of 125

insights.claim: Plastic pollution measures such as bans on single-use bags and straws are the most frequently reported national actions on the pollution target, making visible consumer-facing bans the political path of least resistance.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Governments favour low-cost, high-visibility plastic bans over costly nutrient and pesticide reform - packaging and single-use plastics carry the concentrated regulatory risk.
insights.locator: Measures to address plastic pollution

insights.claim: A major challenge in advancing pollution goals is fairly managing impacts on food security and livelihoods, and several countries cite lack of national funding, with some developing countries flagging poor wastewater-treatment infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Wastewater and nutrient-management infrastructure in developing economies is a named, funded-gap sector for development-finance deployment.

insights.claim: Two-thirds of national targets aligned with the invasive species target show no significant or insufficient progress, fewer than one-third are on track and just 1% have been achieved.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Biosecurity commitments are largely unmet, leaving agricultural and forestry supply chains exposed to invasive-pest shocks.
insights.locator: Two-thirds of national targets aligned with target 6

insights.claim: Only 30% of countries set a numeric goal for reducing invasive species, and countries argue a specific reduction target is challenging because many invasive species go unnoticed for years before impacts become apparent.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Detection lag makes the 50% reduction target structurally unverifiable - early-detection and border-interception systems are the actionable investment, not targets.
